Introduction to Anemia

Red Cell Indices:

•Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV): It is the average volume of the red blood cell expressed in femtoliters. Packed cell volume (PCV)

–MCV 𝑥= RBCs count (X 1012 /𝐿)

–The normal MCV is 78-96 fL

–In electronic counters the MCV is determined by pulse height analysis.

•Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH): It is the average Hemoglobin mass in the red blood cell expressed in picograms. Hb concentration (g/L)

–MCH 𝑥= RBCs count (X 1012 /𝐿)

–The normal MCH is 27-32 pg

–In electronic counters the MCH is calculated.

•Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC): It is the average Hb concentration of the red blood cell expressed in g/L Hb concentration (g/L)

–MCHC 𝑥= Packed cell volume (PCV)

–The normal MCHC is 31-35 g/L

–In electronic counters the MCHC is calculated.

•Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW): It is a measure of variation of red cell size or anisocytosis.

–In electronic counters it is derived from the pulse height analysis and can be expressed either as a coefficient of variation (CV) (%) of the RBCs volume or as the standard deviation (in fL).

–The normal RDW as coefficient of variation is 11.5-14.5 % and as standard deviation is 39 - 46 fl. 3

Anemia

•Definition: Itis a state of decreased red cell mass of blood leading to decreased oxygen carrying capacity of body.

•Classification: I-Morphological classification: 1-Normocytic Normochromic anemia: a decrease in hemoglobin, PCV and RBCs count with normal MCV, MCH, MCHC. The most common causes are: a)Hemolytic anemia b)Post-hemorrhagic anemia in acute blood loss. c)Anemia of chronic disorder b)Aplastic anemia. c)Bone marrow infiltration d)Myelodysplastic syndrome e)Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia 2-Microcytic Hypochromic anemia: a decrease in hemoglobin, PCV and may be RBCs count with low MCV, MCH, MCHC. The most common causes are: a)Iron deficiency. b)Thalassemia. c)Sideroblastic anemia. d)Some unstable hemoglobinopathies e)HbC and HbE. f)Congenital atransferrinemia g)Anemia of chronic disorders h)Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria 3-Macrocytic anemia: a decrease in hemoglobin, PCV and RBCs count with High MCV. The most common causes are: i-Megaloblastic anemia (associated with pancytopenia) a)Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency 4

Iron metabolism

•Definition of iron metabolism: It is the set of chemical reactions maintaining homeostasis of iron at both the systemic and cellular level.

•Distribution of body iron:

–Total body iron is 3-5 gm. (♂ 50 mg/kg, ♀ 40 mg/kg).

–Essential iron: myoglobin and enzymes is not available for erythropoiesis.

•Function of iron 1-Hb: For gas transport 2- Enzymes:

–Cyclooxygenase: Prostaglandin synthesis.

–Cytochromes oxidase (a, b, c) and succinate dehydrogenase: electron transport pathway.

–Cytochrome P450: hydroxylation reactions

–Catalase and lactoperoxidase: peroxide breakdown.

–Tryptophan pyrrolase: oxidation of tryptophan.

–Ribonucleotide reductase: a key enzyme for DNA synthesis. 11

–Iron sulphur proteins: xanthine oxidase, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide dehydrogenase and aconitase. 3- Integrity of epithelial cells. 4- Myoglobin:

–Local tissue reservoir of O2.

–Facilitates intracellular O2 diffusion in muscles.

–Scavenges free radicals. 5- Mitochondria: citric acid cycle. 6-Nervous tissues: Development, Synaptic activity and Myelination. 7- Immunology:

•Iron intake

○Dietary sources :

–High iron diet: liver – kidney - heart – muscle - brewer’s yeast - wheat germ - egg yolks – oysters - some dried beans - some fruits.

–Intermediate iron diet: Green vegetables – cereals – fish – fowl.

–Low iron diet: milk - milk products - most non-green vegetables.

○Daily requirement: 10-20 mg.

○Average dietary intake: 10-20mg from which 5-10 mg is soluble after digestion. 3 mg are taken by intestinal cells from which 1-2 mg are transferred to circulation (5-10% of intake).

Serum Ferritin:

•Clinical uses: It correlates with tissue iron stores. It has high value in iron deficiency and low value in iron overload

•Disadvantages: 1-Ferritin is an acute phase protein. 2-It increases with tissue damage.

•Normal level: 15-300 μg/L in males, 15-200 μg/L in premenopausal female.

•Causes of high serum Ferritin: Increased body iron stores e.g.: primary hemochromatosis or hemolytic anemia. 27

Iron Deficiency Anemia

The most common anemia Definition: A decreases in the number of red cells and concentration of hemoglobin due to lack of iron

Causes:

1-Chronic Blood Loss of at least 6-8 ml/day (the commonest): a-Menstrual blood loss and blood loss related to pregnancy or labor. b-Gastrointestinal tract: -Benign causes as peptic ulcer, hiatus hernia, esophageal varices, parasites as Ankylostoma and Bilharziases, piles, chronic aspirin use and cow milk intolerance in infants. -Malignant causes as Colorectal, gastric and esophageal carcinoma. c-Others: Hemoptysis, epistaxis, hematuria and hemoglobinuria.

2-Increased iron requirements:

- Infancy: especially with prematurity, infection and delayed mixed feeding - Adolescence

–Pregnancy: Pregnant female needs 280 mg iron for the fetus, 500 mg iron for expansion of maternal red cell mass and 200 mg iron for loss in delivery although iron absorption is increased and iron loss is decreased due to amenorrhea.

–Lactation

3-Decreased iron absorption:

–Malabsorption as in coeliac disease, tropical sprue or glutein induced enteropathy - Gasterectomy and achlorohydria: due to the decreased gastric acid 4-Decreased dietary iron intake: in starvation. Anorexia, malnutrition and vegetarians 36
